summary.text: Big Bang nucleosynthesis is a model for how light nuclei such as helium-4 and lithium-7 formed during the first 20 minutes of the universe.
As the expanding universe cooled, protons and neutrons combined into nuclei, and further expansion stopped the process, setting the initial cosmic abundance of these elements.
It predicts a universe of about 75% hydrogen and 25% helium-4 by mass, and refined models agree well with observations.

items.prompt: After nucleosynthesis ended, nearly all ordinary matter was hydrogen and helium. What kept helium-4 from feeding heavier elements?

options.label: Its nuclei hold together so strongly that they rarely break apart
Its nuclei were too light to ever collide with other nuclei
The universe stopped expanding as soon as helium formed
Its nuclei decayed back into protons almost immediately

items.explain: Helium-4 has a large binding energy, so once formed it is difficult to break apart and incorporate its constituents into heavier nuclei.

items.prompt: Where did elements heavier than lithium come from in appreciable amounts?

options.label: From fusion in the first 20 minutes of the universe
From the annihilation of electrons and positrons
From neutrons decaying after the weak interaction faded
Later, through the formation, evolution and death of stars

items.explain: Elements heavier than lithium were created at later times via stellar nucleosynthesis.

items.prompt: Early calculations in the 1940s and 50s predicted hydrogen and helium but nothing heavier. What roadblock stopped them?

options.label: Protons and neutrons refuse to combine at any temperature
No nuclei exist with masses of 5 or 8 atomic mass units to step through
The universe cooled too slowly for any reaction to occur
Too few neutrons were left once the first stars lit up

items.explain: The mass gap, with no nuclei of masses 5 and 8, meant reactions could not reach higher masses, and Fermi and Turkevich found only hydrogen and helium.

items.prompt: Why could deuterium pile up once the universe cooled below roughly 1 MeV?

options.label: Neutrons had all vanished, so nothing could split it
The universe had stopped expanding and held it together
Photons could no longer break it apart, yet fusion still ran fast
Heavier nuclei were forming faster than it could fuse

items.explain: At that temperature photon energy was too low to break apart deuterium, but the universe was still hot and dense enough for significant fusion.

items.prompt: Measurements of one light isotope in the early universe let scientists infer its density. By the 1990s, what did that density imply?

options.label: There must be mass other than baryons, later called dark matter
There must be far more stars than anyone had counted
The universe must be older than the oldest stars
There must be no helium left to measure at all

items.explain: Deuterium abundance could be used to infer primordial density, and by the 1990s that implied mass other than baryons, an idea called dark matter.

items.prompt: Before nucleosynthesis, neutrons and protons swapped identities through the weak interaction. When those swaps fell out of equilibrium, what happened to neutrons?

options.label: Most fused into helium before any decayed
Most decayed into protons, leaving about one neutron per seven protons
Most were destroyed when photons struck them
Most stayed free and made up half of all matter

items.explain: Neutrons primarily decayed to protons, and the neutron-to-proton ratio fell to around 1/7, setting the starting conditions for light nuclei.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Big Bang nucleosynthesis, or BBN for short, is a model of how light atomic nuclei were made in roughly the first 20 minutes of the universe. The nuclei it covers include ²H, ³He, ⁴He and ⁷Li. In it, protons and neutrons build nuclei while the young universe expands and cools. It is one of the key ideas of standard cosmology. Elements heavier than lithium are instead made in sizeable amounts later on, as stars form, evolve and die.

paragraphs.heading: How the process runs
paragraphs.text: At first, protons and neutrons kept joining into nuclei while those nuclei kept breaking apart, a two-way balance called equilibrium. As BBN went on, the universe grew less dense and its particles grew cooler. As temperature and pressure fell, the balance tipped toward a few light nuclei. Further expansion then stopped the process, fixing the starting amounts of these elements.

paragraphs.heading: Setting the stage
paragraphs.text: At temperatures above about 1–2 MeV, protons and neutrons turned into each other through the weak interaction. As it cooled, those reactions fell out of equilibrium, neutrons mostly decayed into protons, and the ratio of neutrons to protons dropped to around 1/7. BBN got going properly once the temperature fell below roughly 1 MeV. By then the average energy of photons was too low to break deuterium apart as it formed, yet the universe was still hot and dense enough for fusion to run at a good pace, so plenty of deuterium built up.

paragraphs.heading: Why helium wins
paragraphs.text: That deuterium then fused into heavier nuclei: tritium, helium-3, helium-4 and lithium-7. Helium-4 has a large binding energy, so once it forms it is hard to split and to use its parts in anything heavier. As a result, the matter left after BBN is mainly hydrogen and helium. Standard BBN predicts about 75% hydrogen and 25% helium-4 by mass. Deuterium and helium-3 together make up roughly 1 nucleus in 100,000, and lithium-7 about 1 in 1,000,000,000.

paragraphs.heading: Gamow and the mass gap
paragraphs.text: It began with nuclear physicist George Gamow, who thought nuclear reactions might predict Victor Goldschmidt's data on how common each element is. Early in the 1940s he saw that the great heat and pressure nuclear reactions need pointed to an explosion followed by expansion. His student Ralph Alpher worked out an early theory of light-element production, published in the Alpher–Bethe–Gamow paper. When Enrico Fermi and Anthony Turkevich tried specific reactions, they got hydrogen and helium but nothing heavier. The block was a mass gap: no nucleus has a mass of 5 or of 8 atomic mass units, and the reactions needed those steps to climb higher. In 1953 it seemed unbeatable and cast doubt on the whole idea.

paragraphs.heading: Stars versus the Big Bang
paragraphs.text: The rival steady state model, set out in two 1948 papers, one by Fred Hoyle and one by Herman Bondi and Thomas Gold, avoided the mass gap by leaving nuclear processes out at first. In 1957 Hoyle, Margaret and Geoffrey Burbidge, and William Fowler built a detailed model of element-making in stars. It matched almost every element except hydrogen and helium, the very ones the Big Bang got right. After the cosmic microwave background was found in 1965, Jim Peebles used its estimated temperature of 3K in the first detailed calculation of the original isotope amounts, giving 26 to 28% helium. A year later Hoyle, Fowler and Robert Wagoner showed that very light elements need more heat than stars provide, which most scientists read as support for the Big Bang.

paragraphs.heading: Deuterium and dark matter
paragraphs.text: From 1972 the Copernicus satellite measured deuterium amounts accurately. Early deuterium production depends more strongly on the density of baryons than helium-3 production does, so the deuterium count could reveal that early density. By the 1990s further measurements showed this density meant there had to be mass other than baryons, an idea that came to be called dark matter. Refined models now agree well with the observed amounts of these light elements.
